displayTitle: The Asymmetry of Volatility Dissipation and Rationality in the Market

content.fullText: In this lecture, we are going to examine what happens in the market after a high volatility move. If we think about volatility for a second, we will realize that is the opposite of price fluctuation. In every financial market on the planet, price tends to rise slowly and drop quickly, and that's not an accident. That happens because there is an asymmetry between certainty and uncertainty. What I mean by this is that certainty is very fragile and can dissipate in a matter of seconds. Uncertainty, on the other hand, is much more stable, and it doesn't dissipate so easily. Let me give you a practical example of this. If everything is okay in the market and prices are naturally rising because the economy is going well and companies are growing, for example, price doesn't skyrocket all at once. It slowly rises. However, if an unprecedented event suddenly happens, like we are seeing right now with the coronavirus and the oil crisis, markets drop quickly. This is why I said that volatility is the inverse of price fluctuation. Price fluctuation rises slowly and drops quickly. Volatility rises quickly and drops slowly. Another way of visualizing this situation is that the natural world has entropy, which is the tendency of things to go out of order. That means that a constant effort must be made just to maintain things working normally. That's why it's difficult to make a company grow and it's very easy to go bankrupt, for example. Yet another way of thinking about this is that it is much easier to demolish a house than it is to build it. To build a house, you need a lot of money, you need intellectual capital, you need a tremendous amount of work, and everything must go according to plan in the end. To demolish the house, you just need a bulldozer. This is precisely the reason why after a high volatility and irrational move in the market, we can expect a low volatility and rational move that is relatively easy to trade compared to the wildness of a downward market. Just as a parenthesis, markets can skyrocket in the very short term in very low timeframes due to the nature of speculation, but not in higher timeframes. In this chart, we can see a good example of what happens after a high volatility move. You can observe that in the 1-2 vector, the market goes straight down with a tremendous amount of volatility. One detail here is that price tends to get stretched out in the end of a move like that, as we can see in low number two. Notice how the last bar really accelerates to the downside as if it was making a final thrust to finish the move. Notice that the last bar of the 1-2 vector is larger than the previous five bars. That's obvious once we point it out, but many people fail to notice that in a move like this, especially because people start to panic once they see something like this in the chart. After low number two, price starts to create a minor flow in the opposite direction with a significantly decreased level of volatility. One particular nuance about this scenario is that since the previous down move wiped out everything in its way, the upward minor flow has a good amount of headroom to travel, so to speak. From number two to number five, we can see the formation of a solid low in number four. Another way you can view this is that after the large bar that creates low number two, it's as if the market was restarted in a way. That allows us to trust the minor movements that we can identify in the minor flow after the high volatility move. If we plot a pitchfork using high number three, low number four, and high number five, we will see that the low number six falls right back to the center line of the pitchfork, which is a textbook retracement move of a running flow. The moment where this happens also coincides with the minor supply zone that comes out of low number four. It is from this moment on that we can start looking for an entry for a long trade. But before we do that, let's review the context for this long trade. The first thing that should grab your attention here is that the notion of market trend can change very quickly. We were clearly going down until number two, and it only took a few bars after that for us to identify an upward movement with solid lows. This is why this notion of market trend can be tricky sometimes. However, considering the whole context of how the markets went down, we can be open-minded about the speed of how the apparent trend changes. Once we have the fractal bar in number six, we can plot another pitchfork to attempt catching the edge of where the market will start going high next. By plotting the pitchfork in low number four, high number five, and low number six, we can see that we have a pitchfork that is too steep. The solution for that is to modify the pitchfork. By doing so, we can see that the lower line of the pitchfork catches the lower tails before price starts to go up in the direction of number nine. If you were unable to catch that in real time, the market would give you yet another opportunity before the rise to number nine. If we look carefully, we can find yet another retracement caught by a pitchfork in number eight. But let's just say that you also missed that. The last resort here would be finding the immediate edge right after number eight. We can do this by plotting a small pitchfork using the lowest edge after low number six, high number seven, and low number eight. We can see that this small pitchfork catches the edge after eight with a small frequency shift that, if corrected, would catch the edge near number nine. Number nine is also an interesting situation for a peculiar reason. If we look at the 1-2 vector once again, we'll see that right in the middle there is a small bump. Normally, we wouldn't care about this bump, but the fact that it is in the middle of a powerful move like that makes it important precisely because it's small. In other words, the fact that a small move like that was able to emerge in the middle of the storm of the 1-2 vector says a lot. The inward frequency line that comes out of this small move in the middle of the 1-2 vector represents a possibility for a short trade in number nine, especially after observing that number nine is a market edge, as we saw with the small pitchfork. If we compare the power of sellers coming out of the small bump with the buyers leading into number nine, it's not difficult to see which one of them is more powerful just by looking at the volatility of the bars. Price indeed starts to go down after number nine. If we were trying to catch the edge right after number nine, we could plot a pitchfork using the small bump in the middle of the 1-2 vector, low number two, and high number nine, and then modify the pitchfork. Notice that in this case, the pitchfork would fail to catch the market edge. However, this pitchfork correctly points to an exhaustion in its center line in number ten with a small undershoot. Notice that low number ten falls exactly in the level where the market finally decided to create the vector 8-9. Buyers and sellers were fighting from number two to number eight with a small advantage to the buyers, since we observe an upward flow. But low number eight is where the sellers finally gave up and let the buyers go up to nine. Just like price remembered number eight in number ten, it remembered number nine in number eleven. If we adjust the frequency shift of the pitchfork in the center line, we can see that the upper line of the pitchfork catches number eleven perfectly where there is a fractal bar and a very clear dynamic frequency breakout. It would be fine to go short in number eleven with a stop above number nine and a target in the center line of the pitchfork. But there is a newer pitchfork that can be drawn here using high number nine, low number ten, and high number eleven as the axes. This pitchfork could also give a further perspective on the trade's target. Hopefully, you were able to apprehend how the context given by the volatility of price moves can shape the way we use line work to find good trade opportunities.

keyEvents.description: Initial static view of a Euro/U.S. Dollar candlestick chart. Key price points are labeled with numbers 1 through 11. A sharp, high-volatility downward move is visible between points 1 and 2.
A downward-sloping Andrews Pitchfork is drawn on the chart. Its anchor points are high #3, low #4, and high #5. The chart shows that the subsequent low (#6) touches the median line of this pitchfork.
An upward-sloping Andrews Pitchfork is drawn using anchor points low #4, high #5, and low #6. The resulting tool is shown to be very steep.

The pitchfork is right-clicked and its type is changed to a 'Modified Schiff' pitchfork. This action flattens the tool's angle, and it is shown to effectively contain the price action from point 6 up to point 9.
A smaller, more immediate upward-sloping pitchfork is drawn using the lowest point after #6, high #7, and low #8 as pivots to illustrate an attempt to catch the next move.
A large, downward-sloping Andrews Pitchfork is drawn. The anchor points are a minor high within the 1-2 vector (referred to as a 'small bump'), low #2, and high #9.

The large pitchfork is changed to a Modified Schiff pitchfork. Its median line is shown to align with low #10, and its upper parallel line aligns with high #11, identifying these points as significant structural levels.
A final, new downward-sloping pitchfork is drawn using high #9, low #10, and high #11 as its anchor points. This tool is shown to frame the subsequent downward price action.

semanticAnalysis.mainConcept: The core concept is the cyclical nature of market volatility and its implications for trading. After a high-volatility, irrational price move (like a market crash, illustrated by the 1-2 vector), the market often enters a period of low-volatility, more rational behavior. This subsequent 'minor flow' is characterized by clearer structure and is more predictable, making it an ideal environment for applying technical analysis tools like the Andrews and Modified Schiff Pitchforks to identify high-probability trade setups.
semanticAnalysis.deeperMeaning: The deeper implication is a strategic framework based on context rather than constant prediction. Instead of trying to trade the chaotic, high-volatility phase, traders should exercise patience and wait for the market to 'reset'. This 'restarted' market state offers clearer signals and better risk-reward opportunities. The lecture connects a philosophical understanding of systems (entropy, the difficulty of building vs. the ease of destroying) to market psychology. The 'small bump' within the crash vector is significant not because of its size, but because its very existence represents a point of order within chaos, making it a powerful reference point for future price action (as seen with points 9, 10, and 11). This teaches traders to look for subtle but powerful structural clues left behind by past market behavior.
semanticAnalysis.educationalGoal: The educational objective is to teach traders how to analyze and adapt to different market volatility regimes. The video demonstrates how to move from a macro observation (high-volatility crash) to a micro analysis of the subsequent price action. It provides a practical application of the Pitchfork tool not as a standalone indicator, but as a method for structuring analysis within a specific, well-defined market context (the post-crash, low-volatility recovery). This lesson aims to develop a nuanced understanding of market dynamics, emphasizing context, patience, and the strategic application of analytical tools.
